prompt.context: Your client, SaveRite, is a large grocery retailer who is under pressure from new leadership to improve historically flat profits within the company. They have come to us to help identify the source of this plateau and develop a plan to increase profitability within the company. SaveRite operates national grocery chains with a nationwide presence and operates only in physical retail locations. Growth within the industry is positive. Competition is not experiencing similar declines in profitability. There are no new market entrants. SaveRite buys food from suppliers and sells to customers. The timeline is ASAP.
prompt.question: What is causing SaveRite's historically flat profits, and what plan would you recommend to increase profitability?

clarifying_info.q: Are competitors experiencing the same profitability issues?
clarifying_info.a: No, competitors are not experiencing similar declines in profitability.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any new competitors entering the market?
clarifying_info.a: No new players have entered the market.

clarifying_info.q: Do we know which products are driving the profitability problem?
clarifying_info.a: No information at this time about products driving the profitability problem.

clarifying_info.q: Does SaveRite operate online as well as physical stores?
clarifying_info.a: SaveRite operates only in physical retail locations.

clarifying_info.q: What does SaveRite's value chain look like?
clarifying_info.a: They buy food from suppliers and sell to customers.

exhibits.title: SaveRite Financial Statements
exhibits.shows: Three-year income statement for SaveRite showing revenue and itemized expenses (COGS, Wages, Corp SG&A, Overhead) and EBITDA from 2012 to 2014

exhibits.title: COGS Breakdown by Category
exhibits.shows: Stacked bar charts breaking down COGS into Direct Labor, Shipping Costs, and Purchase Price across four product categories (Fresh/Produce, Dry Commodities, Alcohol, Dairy) for 2012, 2013, and 2014. All costs are in $M.

exhibits.title: Competitive Product Portfolio for Dry Commodities
exhibits.shows: Table showing the number of products carried across National Brand 1, National Brand 2, National Brand 3, and Private Brand in the Dry Commodities category for three grocery chain competitors: Z-Mart, FoodsRUs, and Green Giant

exhibits.title: Customer Willingness to Pay Survey
exhibits.shows: Bar chart comparing customer preferred price (in $) for National Brand vs. Private Brand products across three dry commodity items: Baking Mix, Flour, and Sugar

framework: Revenues: Analyze revenue trends (volume, price, product mix, store count/traffic); identify opportunities to grow foot traffic and customer base; consider store expansion in high-traffic areas

Costs — COGS: Break down cost of goods sold by product category and sub-cost (purchase price from suppliers, shipping, direct labor); identify which category and cost driver is growing disproportionately
Costs — Fixed/Operating: Evaluate fixed costs (rent/lease, capital expenditures for physical locations) and semi-fixed operating costs (wages, corporate SG&A, overhead)
Market & Competition: Assess industry growth trends; benchmark SaveRite's profitability trajectory against competitors to identify whether the issue is internal or market-wide

questions.prompt: Walk me through Exhibit 1. What do you notice about SaveRite's financial performance?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies: (1) Revenue is growing steadily (~5% YoY: $360M -> $378M -> $397M). (2) EBITDA is essentially flat ($165M across all three years) despite revenue growth. (3) COGS is growing much faster than any other line item — increasing by $10M (20%) from 2012 to 2013 and another $12M (20%) from 2013 to 2014, while wages, SG&A, and overhead grow only ~5% YoY consistent with revenue. Exceptional candidates compute the YoY % growth rates without prompting to quantify that COGS is the outlier driving flat profits.

math.setup: Revenue growth: ($378-$360)/$360 = 5% YoY; ($397-$378)/$378 ≈ 5% YoY. COGS growth: ($60-$50)/$50 = 20% YoY; ($72-$60)/$60 = 20% YoY. EBITDA = Revenue - COGS - Wages - Corp SG&A - Overhead.
steps: Revenue CAGR ≈ 5% YoY; COGS CAGR ≈ 20% YoY; all other costs ≈ 5% YoY
math.answer: COGS is growing at 20% YoY — four times the rate of revenue growth — while all other costs track revenue at ~5%. This is the sole driver of flat EBITDA despite top-line growth.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 2, what can you tell me about what is driving the COGS increase?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies: (1) Most COGS components (Fresh/Produce, Alcohol, Dairy, and the labor/shipping sub-lines within Dry Commodities) are growing at modest or stable rates. (2) The Purchase Price for Dry Commodities is the outlier — jumping from $11M in 2012 to $11M in 2013 and then to $18M in 2014, a 64% increase in two years. This is the anomalous driver within COGS. Exceptional candidates ask whether this is an industry-wide issue or unique to SaveRite, and note the competitor angle (since the prompt stated competitors are not facing similar issues).

math.setup: Dry Commodities Purchase Price: 2012=$11M, 2013=$11M, 2014=$18M. YoY change 2013->2014: ($18-$11)/$11.
steps: Fresh/Produce total COGS is actually declining (2012: $38M, 2014: $28M)
Dry Commodities total: 2012=$14M, 2013=$15M, 2014=$24M — driven almost entirely by purchase price
math.answer: Purchase price within Dry Commodities spiked 64% from 2013 to 2014, making it the outlier driving COGS growth. All other categories and sub-lines are flat or modestly increasing.

questions.prompt: Your hypothesis is that SaveRite's suppliers are overcharging them for dry commodities. What information would be useful to look at next?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask about competitor purchasing behavior in dry commodities, supplier contracts, or whether competitors share the same suppliers. If the candidate brings up supplier contracts, the interviewer notes this is not an industry-wide issue and competitors share many of the same suppliers — then hands over Exhibit 3. Strong candidates proactively ask about competitor product mix to understand if competitors have found an alternative sourcing strategy.

questions.prompt: Walk me through Exhibit 3. What does it tell you about the dry commodities category?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies: (1) All three competitors carry significantly more Private Brand products than National Brand products in dry commodities. (2) This suggests competitors have deliberately shifted away from national brand suppliers — likely to reduce purchase costs. Exceptional candidates articulate the hypothesis that supplier overcharging drove competitors to private brand migration, and ask for data on customer attitudes or willingness to pay to assess whether SaveRite can do the same.

questions.prompt: Walk me through Exhibit 4. What does it mean for our recommendation?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies: (1) Customer willingness to pay for private brand and national brand dry commodities is essentially identical across Baking Mix ($6), Flour ($4), and Sugar ($5). (2) This implies customers have no meaningful brand preference or loyalty in this category. (3) Therefore SaveRite could switch to private brand without sacrificing revenue, while reducing the purchase price paid to national brand suppliers. Exceptional candidates explicitly connect this to the cost reduction opportunity and frame the strategic recommendation.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways SaveRite could reduce its cost of goods sold within the dry commodities category?

categories.name: Supplier Negotiations
ideas: Renegotiate contracts with current suppliers to lower per-unit purchase prices
Leverage volume commitments in exchange for price concessions
Benchmark supplier pricing against industry comparables to strengthen negotiating position

categories.name: Supplier Diversification
ideas: Build relationships with alternative or regional suppliers offering lower costs
Run competitive bids across multiple suppliers for dry commodity inputs
Dual-source to reduce dependency on a single supplier and increase bargaining power

categories.name: Private Brand Development
ideas: Develop or expand SaveRite's own private label line for dry commodities (flour, sugar, baking mix)
Source private label manufacturing directly from commodity producers
Use private brand margin uplift to fund marketing or price competitiveness elsewhere

categories.name: Inventory & Logistics Optimization
ideas: Reduce order quantities to lower holding and inventory carrying costs
Optimize reorder frequency to reduce spoilage and overstock
Consolidate shipping from multiple suppliers to reduce logistics costs

recommendation: SaveRite should migrate its dry commodities category (flour, sugar, baking mix) to a private brand model. Suppliers are overcharging relative to competitors, and all three major competitors have already shifted to predominantly private brand SKUs in this category.

Customers are indifferent between national and private brands in dry commodities — willingness to pay is identical — so the shift will not sacrifice revenue while significantly reducing purchase costs and restoring EBITDA growth.
risks: Discontinuing national brand dry commodity purchases could damage relationships with suppliers who also provide SaveRite with other food categories, potentially leading to worse terms or supply disruptions across the broader product portfolio.
Private brand execution risk: developing and launching a credible private label line requires upfront investment in product development, packaging, and quality assurance.
If customer perceptions shift or brand loyalty emerges (e.g., through marketing by national brands), private label substitution could face resistance.
next_steps: Evaluate the full portfolio of products supplied by the current dry commodity suppliers to understand the waterfall implications of reducing or discontinuing their dry commodity volumes before making the switch.
Conduct a detailed financial model quantifying the COGS savings from private brand migration versus upfront investment required.
Identify and qualify private label manufacturing partners or co-packers for flour, sugar, and baking mix.
Pilot private brand dry commodities in a subset of stores to validate customer acceptance before full rollout.
